name: Nung (Myanmar)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Sun Hongkai & Liu Guangkun (transl. Thurgood et al.). 2009. A Grammar of Anong: Language Death under Intense Contact (Brill) — full phonology chapter; paywalled, not freely online.

new_statements.quote: There are four tones: high level 55, high falling 53, low falling 31, and high rising 35. There is also an unstable mid-level tone which becomes a high-level tone when influenced by low-falling and high-rising tones, and becomes a low-falling tone when influenced by high-falling and high-level tones. Thus, in my description this mid-level tone has been treated as an environmentally-conditioned variant of other tones. The high-level and low-falling tones have a higher frequency than the other two tones. Tones carry a low functional load in terms of differentiating meaning. [...] A syllable is usually composed of an initial, a final, and a tone [...]; all the syllables have a tone.
new_statements.citation: Sun Hongkai. 1988. Notes on Anong, a new language (transl. Li Fengxiang). Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 11(1): 27-63. DOI 10.15144/LTBA-11.1.27

new_statements.rule_in_words: Anong is described as a four-tone language (55, 53, 31, 35, with a conditioned mid tone) in which every syllable carries a tone; the sketch says nothing about word stress or accent at all, so no stress rule can be extracted. The only hint of prominence asymmetry is that prefixes are called 'reduced syllables' with simple vowels and no finals (p. 36).
new_statements.exceptions: Tones have low functional load; unstable mid tone is treated as an allotone.
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/word level; citation forms from the Mugujia Township, Fugong County (Yunnan) variety as recorded by Sun in 1960s-80s.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 1988 describes Anong as spoken in Mugujia Township, Fugong County, Nujiang, Yunnan (the Chinese side; Glottolog nung1282 'Nung (Myanmar)' = Anong/Anung [nun], countries CN;MM). The Myanmar variety (Khwingsang/Kwingsang) is not described in any opened source; Shintani 2018 covers it. No separate glottocode for the Myanmar dialect.

There is also an unstable mid-level tone which becomes a high-level tone when influenced by low-falling and high-rising tones, and becomes a low-falling tone when influenced by high-falling and high-level tones. Thus, in my description this mid-level tone has been treated as an environmentally-conditioned variant of other tones. sources.note: SOUND SYSTEM (pp. 27-34): consonants, finals, III Tones (p. 33: four tones 55/53/31/35 plus an unstable mid tone treated as conditioned variant; 'Tones carry a low functional load in terms of differentiating meaning'), IV Syllables (every syllable has a tone). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the 37-page article (scanned grep stress|accent = 0 hits); prefixes are called 'reduced syllables' (p. 36) but no prominence statement.
